title: How does AQE dynamically change join strategies — after an earlier stage executes and Spark discovers the actual table size is small enough, it can switch from a shuffle join to a broadcast join — and what is the local shuffle reader optimization?
shortTitle: How AQE dynamically changes join strategies and the local shuffle reader

s1_definition.profdef: AQE dynamically changes join strategies by observing the actual size of a join input after an earlier stage has executed, and if one side turns out small enough to fit under the broadcast threshold, it converts a planned shuffle join, such as sort-merge, into a broadcast hash join, which ships the small side to every executor and avoids shuffling the large side. The local shuffle reader is a related optimization: when AQE converts a sort-merge join to a broadcast join, the shuffle that was already written for the large side can be read locally on each executor without a network fetch, since broadcast join no longer needs the data repartitioned across the cluster.
s1_definition.analogy: Two teams at the National Bank of India plan to combine their customer lists by doing a full, slow re-sort so matching names line up — that is a shuffle join. But before they start, AQE checks the actual lists and notices one team's list is tiny, just a single page. Instead of the heavy re-sort, AQE simply photocopies that one page and hands it to everyone, so each clerk matches against the copy locally — that is a broadcast join, and it skips the re-sort entirely. The local shuffle reader is the follow-on cleverness: because the big list no longer needs re-sorting across teams, each clerk just reads the portion already sitting on their own desk instead of fetching pages from other desks across the office.
s1_definition.oneliner: AQE flips a shuffle join to a broadcast join once it sees a side is actually small, eliminating the big shuffle, and the local shuffle reader then lets each executor read its already-written shuffle data locally instead of over the network.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** AQE dynamically changes join strategies by observing the actual size of a join input after an earlier stage has executed, and if one side turns out small enough to fit under the broadcast threshold, it converts a planned shuffle join, such as sort-merge, into a broadcast hash join, which ships the small side to every executor and avoids shuffling the large side. The local shuffle reader is a related optimization: when AQE converts a sort-merge join to a broadcast join, the shuffle that was already written for the large side can be read locally on each executor without a network fetch, since broadcast join no longer needs the data repartitioned across the cluster.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Two teams at the National Bank of India plan to combine their customer lists by doing a full, slow re-sort so matching names line up — that is a shuffle join. But before they start, AQE checks the actual lists and notices one team's list is tiny, just a single page. Instead of the heavy re-sort, AQE simply photocopies that one page and hands it to everyone, so each clerk matches against the copy locally — that is a broadcast join, and it skips the re-sort entirely. The local shuffle reader is the follow-on cleverness: because the big list no longer needs re-sorting across teams, each clerk just reads the portion already sitting on their own desk instead of fetching pages from other desks across the office.

**One line to remember:** AQE flips a shuffle join to a broadcast join once it sees a side is actually small, eliminating the big shuffle, and the local shuffle reader then lets each executor read its already-written shuffle data locally instead of over the network.

sections.s2_technical:
Join strategy selection normally happens in Catalyst before the job runs, using size estimates. If both sides are estimated to be large, Catalyst picks a shuffle join like sort-merge, which repartitions both sides by the join key across the cluster so matching keys meet in the same partition. If one side is estimated small, it instead picks a broadcast hash join, which sends the entire small side to every executor and joins locally against each partition of the large side, avoiding any shuffle of the large side. The trouble is that estimates are often wrong — especially after filters and aggregations earlier in the plan can shrink a table dramatically below its original size.

AQE fixes this by deferring the final decision. After an earlier stage executes, Spark knows the real size of its output. At the point where the join is about to run, AQE compares the actual size of each side against the broadcast threshold, and if a side that was estimated large is actually small enough, it rewrites the physical plan to a broadcast join instead of the planned sort-merge. This is extremely common in star-schema banking queries where a dimension table looks large statically but is tiny after a filter, and the switch turns an expensive two-sided shuffle into a cheap broadcast.

The local shuffle reader is the complementary optimization that makes this conversion even cheaper. When AQE changes a sort-merge join into a broadcast join, the large side had already been shuffled, meaning its data was written out partitioned by the join key. A broadcast join does not require that repartitioning, so instead of each task fetching its shuffle blocks from across the network, AQE uses a local shuffle reader: each executor reads the shuffle output that is already on its own local disk, with no network transfer. This removes the network cost of the now-unnecessary repartition while reusing the work already done.

A senior nuance is that this whole mechanism is why you can keep the broadcast threshold at a sensible value and let AQE opportunistically broadcast whenever runtime sizes allow, rather than manually hinting every join. It also interacts with the other AQE features: a join that stays a shuffle join still benefits from coalescing and skew handling, while a join that flips to broadcast benefits from the local shuffle reader. The caution is that broadcasting a side that is actually too large can cause executor out-of-memory errors, so the threshold must respect executor memory, and AQE only broadcasts when the measured size is genuinely under it. In the bank, these runtime join switches quietly removed many of the heavy shuffles in our reporting queries whenever a filter made a dimension table small, with no query changes.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Catalyst planned a slow sort-merge shuffle join from a stale large estimate. This is exactly what dynamic join switching corrects at runtime.

Problem 2 — After a filter the dimension table is actually tiny. This is exactly when switching to a broadcast join pays off.

Problem 3 — The large side was already shuffled; fetching it over the network is wasteful once we broadcast. This is exactly what the local shuffle reader avoids.

The mini-project models this in Java. A `JoinPlanner` starts with a sort-merge plan from an estimate. An `AqeJoinOptimizer` checks the actual measured size of the dimension side and, if under the threshold, switches to broadcast and enables a local shuffle reader flag for the large side. The demo joins a filtered branch dimension against Rajesh's and Priya's transaction fact data and prints the plan transitions.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a branch dimension estimated at five hundred megabytes but actually only eight megabytes after a filter, and a transaction fact table of twenty gigabytes. The broadcast threshold is ten megabytes.

Step 1: The initial Catalyst-style planner uses the estimate of five hundred megabytes for the dimension, which exceeds the ten-megabyte threshold, so it plans a sort-merge shuffle join that would repartition both sides across the cluster.

Step 2: An earlier stage runs and applies the filter, after which the real size of the dimension side is known to be eight megabytes.

Step 3: AQE compares the actual dimension size, eight megabytes, against the ten-megabyte threshold. Because it is now under the threshold, AQE rewrites the plan from sort-merge to a broadcast join, which will ship the tiny dimension to every executor and avoid shuffling the twenty-gigabyte fact table.

Step 4: Because the fact table had already been shuffled under the original sort-merge plan, and a broadcast join no longer needs that repartition, AQE enables the local shuffle reader so each executor reads its already-written shuffle output from local disk without fetching across the network.

Step 5: The final plan is a broadcast join with the local shuffle reader enabled, turning an expensive two-sided shuffle into a cheap broadcast plus local reads.

Step 6: The journey shows the decision deferred until real sizes were known, the heavy shuffle of the large fact table eliminated, and the previously written shuffle reused locally — all without changing the query.

```text
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] initial plan: SORT_MERGE (estimate 500000000B exceeds threshold)
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] after initial plan: strategy=SORT_MERGE
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] AQE: actual branch_dim size 8000000B <= threshold → switch to BROADCAST
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] AQE: enable local shuffle reader for 'txn_fact' — read already-written shuffle on each executor, no network
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] final: strategy=BROADCAST, localShuffleReader=true
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Catalyst (estimate): branch_dim=500MB, txn_fact=20GB → SORT_MERGE (shuffle both)
    │
    ▼  earlier stage runs filter → ACTUAL branch_dim = 8MB
  AQE compares actual 8MB vs 10MB threshold → under!
    │
    ├─ switch SORT_MERGE → BROADCAST
    │     ship 8MB branch_dim to every executor, join locally
    │     NO 20GB fact shuffle across network
    │
    └─ enable LOCAL SHUFFLE READER
          txn_fact already shuffled → read local blocks, no network fetch
    │
    ▼
  Final: BROADCAST join + local shuffle reader (big shuffle eliminated)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
AQE dynamically changes join strategies to fix the fact that Catalyst must pick a join algorithm before the job runs, from size estimates that are frequently wrong after filters and aggregations. Normally, if both sides are estimated large, Catalyst picks a shuffle join like sort-merge that repartitions both sides by the join key so matching keys meet; if one side is estimated small, it picks a broadcast hash join that ships the small side everywhere and avoids shuffling the large side. The problem is a dimension table can look large statically but become tiny after a filter earlier in the plan.

AQE defers the final decision. After an earlier stage executes, the real size of its output is known, so at the point where the join is about to run, AQE compares the actual size of each side against the broadcast threshold, and if a side that was estimated large is actually small enough, it rewrites a planned sort-merge join into a broadcast join. This eliminates the expensive two-sided shuffle in exactly the common star-schema case where a filter shrinks a dimension below the threshold. The local shuffle reader is the complementary optimization: when AQE makes this switch, the large side had already been shuffled, written out partitioned by the join key, but a broadcast join no longer needs that repartition, so instead of each task fetching shuffle blocks across the network, each executor reads the shuffle output already sitting on its own local disk, removing the network cost while reusing the work.

In my project at the National Bank of India these runtime join switches quietly removed many heavy shuffles from our reporting queries whenever a filter made a dimension table small, and the local shuffle reader meant we did not even pay to re-fetch the large side. The practical lesson is that you can keep the broadcast threshold at a sensible value and let AQE opportunistically broadcast whenever the measured runtime sizes allow, instead of hand-hinting every join. The one caution I always give is that broadcasting a side that is actually too large causes executor out-of-memory errors, so the threshold must respect executor memory, and AQE only switches when the genuinely measured size is under it.
